lines: Thirty-two slots out of two hundred ready tasks sounds like a small decision. It decides the whole pipeline's finish time, because every slot you fill with the wrong task is a slot the right task didn't get.
Before you answer, separate two different questions: which task the rule runs first, and which task actually finishes the pipeline sooner. They are not always the same question.
answer: The fan-out runs first, because the default rule counts tasks below, not how long the chain below is.
But watch the chain's own finish time in the next few steps. With only these two competing, there turns out to be enough slack that the order barely matters.

lines: Nothing on this screen is new to you. What's worth noticing is how little of it survives once a real scheduler gets involved — everything after this step is about what changes when the graph stops sitting still.

Three shapes, three roles: a chain you'll track all topic, a fan-out that competes with it for workers, and a third branch that's longer than either but doesn't show up until later. Hold onto that third one.
Notice the fan-out's total work is small — five short tasks — while the chain is short but each step is long. Count and duration are already pulling in different directions.
Read the default slowly: a sum over descendants, not a maximum over any chain. That's the whole surprise of this topic, stated in one sentence before any code runs.

A set, not a list, is the detail worth sitting with. If a descendant were counted once per path reaching it, a diamond-shaped DAG would quietly inflate its own priority every time you added a redundant edge.
The source doesn't call this out as a design choice worth justifying. It's just the obvious way to answer 'how much depends on this,' which is exactly the topic's point.
The rule picked correctly, exactly as predicted. Now look at what that prediction didn't promise: a different finish time for the thing you actually care about.
Running the fan-out first used up worker time the chain wasn't going to need yet anyway. The ranking changed; the schedule's shape around it absorbed the difference.
This is the fix a user actually has to apply by hand — set every task's own weight to its own duration. Airflow doesn't do this for you; there's no separate critical-path rule.
And it works, for this one pair: the chain now outranks the fan-out. Don't conclude yet that it always will.
Here's the branch you were told to hold onto. Add it back in, and the clean story from two steps ago breaks.

The duration-weighted rule isn't wrong here, it's just not aimed at what you assumed it was aimed at: a sum of durations is still a sum, not a longest path, and a sum can lose to a shorter sum that happens to sit on the chain you're watching.

Take the workers away entirely and the scheduling problem disappears — what's left is pure graph structure. The longest chain by duration is the floor nothing can beat, no matter how clever the ready-queue rule is.
Notice which chain that is. It isn't the one this whole topic has been narrating around.
This bound doesn't care which rule you used, or whether your rule was any good at guessing the critical path. It's a worst case over every possible ready-queue order, including a bad one.
Both measured runs sit well inside it. That's expected — the bound is loose on purpose, a guarantee, not a prediction.
Both of these detect the exact same cycle. The question is which one was built to remember how it got there.
One of them is just counting. The other is tracking a path.
answer: The depth-first search names the one faulty edge; Kahn's algorithm only shows the whole stuck group.

Kahn's algorithm never asks which edge is the problem; it just reports who's still stuck when it runs out of ready tasks. The depth-first search was watching the exact path it came in on, so it's the only one that can name an edge.

lines: Carry forward the one habit this topic was really about: ask what a rule is actually optimizing before you trust that it's optimizing the thing you care about.
